# Building and installation {#build}

> **Building a device?** Follow the step-by-step **[device build guide](build/)**: parts and
> bill of materials, circuit boards, clock battery, camera, wiring, assembly, flashing, and the
> DWARPH-QC check. This chapter covers the software side.

The three software components install independently: the **firmware** has to be compiled and flashed onto each device, the **Commander** is installed once on the machine you want to drive the devices from, and **DWARPH-CV** goes on whichever machine analyses the images. You do not need the firmware toolchain to run the Commander, or vice versa. The **hub** is optional, for large set-ups only (Section \@ref(build-hub)).

## Firmware {#build-firmware}

### Requirements {-}

* **ESP-IDF**, version 4.1 or newer, set up per the [Espressif getting-started guide](https://docs.espressif.com/projects/esp-idf/en/stable/esp32/get-started/index.html)
* A target board based on the **ESP32-S3** (developed against the Seeed Studio XIAO Sense ESP32S3)
* A USB cable and, on Linux, permission to access the serial port (typically membership of the `dialout` group)

Third-party components are pulled automatically by the IDF Component Manager from `main/idf_component.yml`: `espressif/esp32-camera`, `espressif/mdns` and `hayschan/autopid_for_esp_idf`. A modified OV5640 autofocus driver is vendored in `components/`.

### Build and flash {-}

With the ESP-IDF environment activated:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/DWARPHs/DWARPH-firmware.git
cd DWARPH-firmware

idf.py set-target esp32s3
idf.py build
idf.py -p <PORT> flash monitor
```

`<PORT>` is the device's serial port --- `/dev/ttyACM0` or `/dev/ttyUSB0` on Linux, `COM3` or similar on Windows. Leave `monitor` off if you do not want to attach to the serial console; `Ctrl+]` exits it.

### Configuration {-}

WiFi credentials and the image capture interval are read from the device's `schedule.json` (see Section \@ref(schedules)), not compiled in, so the same binary can be flashed to every device in a fleet. Note that some settings still live in headers under `main/`, and are being migrated to the configuration file.

Once a device is running, subsequent updates can be pushed over the network through the `/api/firmware/upload` endpoint instead of over USB.

## Commander {#build-gui}

### Requirements {-}

* **Python 3** with Tk support (on some Linux distributions Tk is a separate package, e.g. `python-tk` or `python3-tk`)
* The packages pinned in `requirements.txt`: `zeroconf`, `Pillow`, `opencv-python`, `matplotlib`, `paho-mqtt`, `pyserial` and `esp-idf-monitor`

### Install and run {-}

```bash
git clone https://github.com/DWARPHs/DWARPH-commander.git
cd DWARPH-commander

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate        # Windows: .\.venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

python app.py
```

On Windows, `run_app.bat` does the equivalent in one step.

The Commander needs to be on the **same local network** as the devices, and mDNS traffic must not be blocked between them --- this is the usual reason a device that is plainly powered up never appears in the grid. Discovery starts automatically in the background when the app launches.

If you have no hardware to hand, the `Mock Device` toggle shows a fixed demo card so you can explore the interface.

## DWARPH-CV {#build-cv}

### Requirements {-}

* **Python 3.10** or newer
* **PyTorch**: a CUDA build if the machine has an NVIDIA GPU (see [pytorch.org](https://pytorch.org/get-started/locally/)); the CPU build works too, more slowly

### Install and run {-}

```bash
pip install torch torchvision --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu126   # or .../whl/cpu

git clone https://github.com/DWARPHs/DWARPH-CV.git
cd DWARPH-CV
pip install -e .                 # segmentation and ring reference
pip install -e '.[train]'        # optional: training
pip install -e '.[annotate]'     # optional: SAM 2.1 annotator (NVIDIA GPU needed)

dwarph-cv segment --input /path/to/Device_mirror/C4E408 --output preds   # masks + areas.csv
dwarph-cv ring --root /path/to/Device_mirror/C4E408                       # camera distance and tilt
```

The first `segment` run downloads the released model from Zenodo and caches it in `~/.cache/dwarph_cv/`. Use `--weights path/to/model.pt` for your own model. `dwarph-cv --help` lists all commands.

## MQTT broker {#build-broker}

MQTT is **optional**. Without it, devices are still fully controllable over REST; what you lose is the once-per-second live update on the device cards.

To enable it, run an MQTT broker reachable by both the devices and the Commander --- [Mosquitto](https://mosquitto.org/) is the usual choice, and the Commander repository ships a `mosquitto.conf` to start from --- then add the broker fields to each device's schedule as described in Section \@ref(mqtt).

## DWARPH-hub (optional) {#build-hub}

Only for large set-ups (Section \@ref(hub-module)). A single lab does not need it.

### Deploy {-}

You need:

* a **Linux server** with Docker and the compose plugin, ports 80 and 443 open: 4 GB of memory for
  real use (2 GB is enough to try it);
* a **domain** with two DNS records pointing at the server, for example `hub.example.org` (the
  hub) and `auth.example.org` (signing in);
* an **S3 bucket** (e.g. Linode or AWS object storage) and an access key **limited to that
  bucket**.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/DWARPHs/DWARPH-hub.git && cd DWARPH-hub
cp deploy/prod.env.example deploy/prod.env      # host names, bucket, key id
# one secret per file in secrets/ (database, the bucket key's secret, Authentik):
# the commands are in deploy/README.md
docker network create dwarph-edge
docker compose --env-file deploy/prod.env -f docker-compose.edge.yml up -d    # HTTPS
docker compose --env-file deploy/prod.env -f docker-compose.prod.yml up -d --build
curl https://hub.example.org/healthz
```

Then open `https://auth.example.org/if/flow/initial-setup/` **straight away** to set the
administrator's password, create the people's accounts in Authentik, and put yourself in the
group **`dwarph-admins`** (the hub's administrators). A person needs a role on the hub to see
anything: **reader** for people. Machines get the roles below. Backups (a nightly `pg_dump`;
the images are in the bucket) and updates are in the repository's `deploy/README.md`.

### Connect a Commander {-}

Each lab's Commander pushes its device mirror to the hub with a **machine account**:

1. In Authentik, create a service account for the lab and an app password for it, and give it
   the **contributor** role on the hub (`PUT /v1/access/<id>` with `{"role": "contributor"}`).
2. On the lab's computer, put its credentials in `~/.config/dwarph/hub.json` (mode 600):
   `{"issuer": "https://auth.example.org/application/o/dwarph-commander/", "client_id": "dwarph-commander", "username": "...", "password": "..."}`.
3. Push the mirror the Commander keeps:

```bash
python tools/push_mirror.py --hub https://hub.example.org --credentials ~/.config/dwarph/hub.json \
    --mirror /path/to/Device_mirror --jobs 8
```

Pushing is safe to repeat (images already on the hub are skipped) and never changes the mirror.
Each image is checked against its device's checksum before it is sent, and again by the hub
once it is stored; an image without a readable sidecar is not sent. Run it from `cron` to keep
the hub up to date. *(The Commander will do this by itself once it runs as Docker services; the
protocol is `contract/SYNC.md` in the hub's repository.)*

### Connect DWARPH-CV workers {-}

Any computer can analyse the hub's images; one with an NVIDIA GPU does it quickly.

1. Give it a machine account as above, with the **worker** role, and its credentials in
   `~/.config/dwarph/worker.json`.
2. Once, an administrator registers the algorithms this version of DWARPH-CV computes (this
   queues every image for them):
   `dwarph-cv worker --hub https://hub.example.org --credentials admin.json --register-only`.
3. Run the worker:

```bash
dwarph-cv worker --hub https://hub.example.org --credentials ~/.config/dwarph/worker.json
```

It takes images newest first, downloads each one once, runs the ring detection and the
segmentation, and sends back the results and the mask; with nothing left to do it waits for new
images. Start as many workers as you like, on as many computers. To keep one running permanently,
install it as a service with `tools/worker/` in DWARPH-CV: the service updates DWARPH-CV whenever
it restarts. When a new ring or model version is released, register it with `--register-only
--retire-older`. Every worker then moves to the new version by itself, every image is analysed
again, and the old results are kept.
